evidence.title: AI-assisted vs. textbook-based vs. blended learning for acute abdomen diagnosis: a retrospective cohort study of emergency interns
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy with blended versus AI-assisted learning
evidence.effect: Accuracy was 87.1% (blended) versus 82.4% (AI-assisted); AI-assisted versus blended OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209. Unaided skill retention was not assessed.
evidence.quote: The difference between AI-assisted and blended learning was not statistically significant (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209).

evidence.title: The implementation of computer-aided detection in an initial endoscopy training improves the quality measures of trainees' future colonoscopies: a retrospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: adenoma and sessile lesion detection rate
evidence.effect: The AI-trained group had a significantly improved adenoma detection rate by 5.3% and sessile lesion detection rate by 5.4%.
evidence.quote: AI-trained group had also a significantly improved adenoma detection rate (ADR) by 5.3% (95% CI: 2.9-7.6%) and sessile lesion detection rate (SDR) by 5.4% (95% CI: 3.8-7.0%).

evidence.title: Implementation of Artificial Intelligence-Powered Patient Simulation for Communication Training in a Telehealth Transitional Care Program
evidence.venue: Simulation in healthcare : journal of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Communication rubric scores during real telehealth patient encounters
evidence.effect: Rubric scores improved by 24% for inpatient, 19% for postoperative, and 37% for emergency department pathways (P < 0.001 for each), with sustained median shifts.
evidence.quote: Total rubric scores improved: inpatient by 24% (P < 0.001), postoperative by 19% (P < 0.001), and emergency department by 37% (P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Teacher–Student–Machine Interaction Autonomous Learning: A Structured LLM-Integrated Framework for Developing Independent Clinical Reasoning in Residency Training
evidence.outcome: Unassisted clinical reasoning after structured LLM-integrated residency training vs traditional teaching
evidence.effect: Unassisted clinical reasoning scores 7.32 ± 2.30 vs 5.12 ± 1.66 (P < 0.001); SP exam 80.88 vs 78.71 (P = 0.025); TSM-AL residents performed better without LLM than with it.
evidence.quote: In the unassisted final examination, the TSM-AL group demonstrated significantly higher clinical reasoning scores (7.32 ± 2.30 vs 5.12 ± 1.66, P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted training for rib fracture interpretation: a prospective study in undergraduate medical students
evidence.venue: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES
evidence.outcome: skill retention after AI withdrawal
evidence.effect: S3 declined versus S2, but baseline-to-S3 accuracy +13.3%, p = 0.010 and precision +13.7%, p = 0.010.
evidence.quote: Performance in S3 declined compared to S2 but remained higher than baseline for accuracy (+ 13.3%, p = 0.010) and precision (+ 13.7%, p = 0.010) compared to baseline.

evidence.title: Comparing individual and peer-supported ChatGPT use in nursing case analysis: Effects on nursing diagnostic skills and cognitive load in a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Development of nursing diagnostic skills during ChatGPT-supported clinical education
evidence.effect: Among 91 students, diagnostic skills improved after intervention, but the interaction among instructional groups was not significant (p = .936). ChatGPT-supported conditions showed no statistically significant advantage over traditional instruction.
evidence.quote: Although students' nursing diagnostic skills improved after the intervention, we did not observe a significant interaction effect among the groups (p = .936).

evidence.title: Impact of Introducing Artificial Intelligence on Colonoscopy: A Retrospective Study on Potential Benefits and Drawbacks
evidence.outcome: Endoscopist adenoma and polyp detection rates without CAD, before versus after CAD introduction
evidence.effect: Without CAD, ADR fell from 31.6% to 13.5% (p<0.001) and PDR from 39.8% to 18.2% (p<0.001) after CAD introduction, suggesting reliance on CAD and lapses in independent detection.
evidence.quote: ADR (31.6% vs. 13.5%, p < 0.001) and PDR (39.8% vs. 18.2%, p < 0.001) were significantly lower in the post-intervention non-CAD group than in the pre-intervention non-CAD group.

evidence.title: Long-term impact of computer-aided adenoma detection: a prospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Change in adenoma detection rate (CUSUM) in non-CADe procedures over time, as a measure of deskilling
evidence.effect: No deskilling seen. High detectors had accelerated learning curves without CADe; low detectors showed no significant change. Detection rate without CADe was maintained and did not decline.
evidence.quote: After CADe implementation, the detection rate in procedures performed without CADe was maintained and did not decline over time.

evidence.title: The implementation of computer-aided detection in an initial endoscopy training improves the quality measures of trainees' future colonoscopies: a retrospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: Independent (non-AI) colonoscopy quality of CADe-trained vs conventionally trained endoscopists
evidence.effect: AI-trained endoscopists, performing without AI, had higher ADR (35.5% vs 30.3%; +5.3%, 95% CI 2.9–7.6) and SDR (12.5% vs 7.1%; +5.4%, 95% CI 3.8–7.0); similar CIR.
evidence.quote: AI-enhanced training improved ADR by 5.3% and SDR by 5.4% (95% CI: 2.9–7.6%, and 3.8–7.0%, respectively) in high-power analysis (98.5–100%).

evidence.title: Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study
evidence.outcome: Change in adenoma detection rate of non-AI colonoscopy before vs after AI exposure
evidence.effect: ADR of standard colonoscopy fell from 28.4% (226/795) to 22.4% (145/648), absolute difference -6.0% (95% CI -10.5 to -1.6; p=0.0089); AI exposure OR 0.69 (0.53-0.89).
evidence.quote: The ADR of standard colonoscopy decreased significantly from 28·4% (226 of 795) before to 22·4% (145 of 648) after exposure to AI, corresponding with an absolute difference of -6·0% (95% CI -10·5 to -1·6; p=0·0089).

evidence.title: Physicians' perceptions of how digital-intelligent medical technology reshapes job characteristics: a qualitative study
evidence.outcome: Physician-perceived skill degradation and technical dependency from digital-intelligent medical technology
evidence.effect: Interviewed physicians described technical dependency and skill degradation risks as new job demands; no prevalence figures reported.
evidence.quote: Challenges such as technical dependency, operational complexity, and ethical responsibility arising from digital-intelligent medical technologies impose new job demands on physicians, exacerbating burnout and skill degradation risks.

evidence.title: Radiographers' role in the age of AI: A qualitative comparative multi case study
evidence.outcome: Radiographer concerns about deskilling and loss of identity from AI
evidence.effect: Participants viewed AI as both a facilitator and a potential threat to core tasks, raising concerns about deskilling and loss of identity; maintaining competence was highlighted as critical.
evidence.quote: Participants viewed AI as both a facilitator of daily work and a potential threat to core tasks, raising concerns about deskilling and loss of identity.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (section leaders, researchers, department managers)

evidence.title: Stakeholder Perspectives of Implementation Barriers of Artificial Intelligence in Eye Care: A qualitative framework-based study
evidence.venue: Ophthalmic & physiological optics : the journal of the British College of Ophthalmic Opticians (Optometrists)
evidence.outcome: Stakeholder-perceived barrier of AI over-reliance and clinician deskilling
evidence.effect: Leaders most often cited the 'individuals' domain, expressing risk of over-reliance on AI and consequent clinician deskilling. This is a perceived concern from interviews, not a measured occurrence.
evidence.quote: Leaders were focused on the innovation deliverers: expressing the potential risk of over-reliance on the innovation and the subsequent consequence of clinician deskilling.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Use and Training Needs Among Rheumatologists: An APLAR Young Rheumatologists International Survey
evidence.outcome: Concern about loss of traditional clinical skills from LLM reliance
evidence.effect: 81.1% of both users and nonusers shared concerns regarding potential loss of traditional clinical skills.
evidence.quote: Although both groups shared concerns regarding the potential loss of traditional clinical skills (81.1%), active users significantly favored the integration of mandatory LLMs training into core rheumatology curricula.

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Over-reliance on device and loss of clinical skills (qualitative)
evidence.effect: Providers reported omitting physical examinations and vital sign checks and worried about losing fundamental clinical skills
evidence.quote: Although the device was widely accepted, the study revealed over-reliance on the device, with some providers substituting essential clinical practices like physical examinations and vital sign checks.

evidence.title: Implementing a Commercial AI Fracture Detection Tool in Health Care Using the Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-Up, Spread, and Sustainability Framework: A Formative Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician deskilling concerns during AI fracture detection implementation
evidence.effect: Deskilling was identified as a major challenge in the qualitative evaluation; no quantitative measure was reported.
evidence.quote: Major challenges comprised limited documentation of Conformité Européenne-marked solutions, deskilling, and misaligned financial incentives.

evidence.title: Current Landscape of Generative AI Use as a Search Engine Among Resident Physicians: Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Association of GenAI use with self-reported behaviors indicative of knowledge collapse or deskilling
evidence.effect: GenAI use was independently associated with favorable behaviors: thorough examination (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 1.18-1.70) and appropriate antimicrobial use (aOR 1.57, 95% CI 1.32-1.87). Only 13% (144/1110) of users relied on GenAI as primary reference for differential diagnoses.
evidence.quote: Although GenAI use was not associated with self-reported behaviors indicative of knowledge collapse at this stage, GenAI literacy among resident physicians in Japan remains limited, particularly among nonusers.

evidence.title: Generative AI dependency and self-perceived clinical decision-making in nursing students: A three-wave longitudinal study of metacognitive awareness as a mediator
evidence.outcome: Within-person association of generative AI dependency with later metacognitive awareness and self-perceived clinical decision-making
evidence.effect: Higher dependency predicted lower metacognitive awareness at next wave (β = -0.18 to -0.21, p < .001); indirect effect on decision-making via metacognition = -0.045, 95% CI [-0.074, -0.019]; direct effect not significant.
evidence.quote: At the within-person level, higher generative artificial intelligence dependency was prospectively associated with lower metacognitive awareness at the subsequent wave (β = -0.18 to -0.21, p < .001).

evidence.title: Healthcare Professionals' Expectations of Medical Artificial Intelligence and Strategies for its Clinical Implementation: A Qualitative Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician concerns about deskilling from medical AI use, from interviews
evidence.effect: Participants mentioned deskilling as a concern about medical AI, alongside workflow distortion, alert fatigue, and unsophisticated algorithms. No frequency was reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: While the participants expressed expectations that medical AI could enhance their patients' outcomes, increase work efficiency, and reduce hospital operating costs, they also mentioned concerns regarding distortions in the workflow, deskilling, alert fatigue, and unsophisticated algorithms.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted training for rib fracture interpretation: a prospective study in undergraduate medical students
evidence.venue: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES
evidence.outcome: Retention of diagnostic skill after AI withdrawal and overreliance concerns among trainees
evidence.effect: After AI withdrawal (S3) performance declined vs S2 but stayed above baseline for accuracy (+13.3%, p=0.010) and precision (+13.7%, p=0.010); 34.6% worried about over-reliance.
evidence.quote: However, slight improvements were still observed, with statistically significant improvements in accuracy (13.3%, p = 0.010) and precision (13.7%, p = 0.010).

evidence.title: A prospective multicenter trial of deep learning auto-segmentation for organs at risk in thoracic radiotherapy
evidence.outcome: Change in manual contouring accuracy over time among less-experienced physicians using AI
evidence.effect: Of 25 less-experienced physicians, 19 (76%) no change, 3 (12%) improved, 3 (12%) declined in manual vDSC.
evidence.quote: In contrast, three (12%) experienced a decline in M-vDSC ( p = 0.042, 0.029, and 0.013), characterized by under- or over-segmentation of clear anatomical boundaries and increased OAR overlap (Supplementary Fig. 21 ).

evidence.title: Comparing individual and peer-supported ChatGPT use in nursing case analysis: Effects on nursing diagnostic skills and cognitive load in a randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Nursing diagnostic skills after ChatGPT-supported vs traditional case-based learning
evidence.effect: Diagnostic skills improved in all groups; no significant group-by-time interaction (p = .936); ChatGPT conditions showed no advantage or disadvantage versus traditional method.
evidence.quote: Although students' nursing diagnostic skills improved after the intervention, we did not observe a significant interaction effect among the groups (p = .936).

commentary.bottom_line: Studies of AI-integrated clinical education show mixed effects on unaided skills, and no study tests whether a health system that assesses deskilling risk tool by tool prevents skill loss. Colonoscopy studies report both declines and gains in unaided detection after AI exposure, which suggests the risk may vary by tool, clinician, and setting.

perspectives.view: Six studies test AI-integrated training, and none tests a health system assessing deskilling risk tool by tool. Two randomized trials in simulated settings disagree. One trial (n=68) found higher unassisted reasoning scores (7.32 vs 5.12), and the other (n=91) found no group difference (p = .936). Small samples, indirect outcomes, and inconsistent results lower certainty to very low.

After CAD introduction, unaided adenoma detection fell from 28.4% to 22.4% in one study and from 31.6% to 13.5% in another. A propensity-matched study found no decline, and CADe-trained endoscopists detected more adenomas without AI (35.5% vs 30.3%). In contouring, 3 of 25 physicians declined. These findings suggest deskilling risk may differ by tool and clinician.

Two tests ran in real workflows. Emergency interns trained with AI assistance reached 82.4% accuracy versus 87.1% with blended learning (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.41–1.16), and unaided retention was not measured. A telehealth program reported rubric gains of 19% to 37% without a comparator. No study measured the staff time or fidelity needed to run deskilling assessments.

No study testing the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one hazard study in such a setting, covering 81 providers at 7 facilities in rural Sierra Leone, found providers omitting physical examinations and vital sign checks while relying on a scanning device. Whether training safeguards work in low-resource settings has not been tested.

The Sierra Leone report of skipped physical examinations and vital sign checks shows that reliance on a device can reach patients directly. The telehealth study, measured on 468 real patient calls, suggests AI-supported training may improve how clinicians communicate with patients, though it lacked a comparator group.

commentary.research_gap: No study evaluates a health system process for assessing deskilling risk before or after an AI tool is deployed, and few education studies measure unaided performance after AI withdrawal in real practice. Prospective studies with comparators that track unaided performance over time, including during AI downtime, and that report cost and staff time would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the six studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only hazard study in such a setting, in rural Sierra Leone with non-English-speaking populations, found providers skipping basic examinations. Health systems serving these populations therefore have no direct evidence on whether deskilling assessments or AI-supported training protect clinician skills in their settings.
